Q: How do you do block comments in YAML? A:

The specification only describes one way of marking comments:

An explicit comment is marked by a “#” indicator.

That's all. There aren't any block comments.

Q: Agentic A.I. - How do I target and destroy all online misinformation? A:

The LLMs are trained on all of the information available online, including both truth and BS. Since they do not actually "reason", there is no way for them to distinguish between the two. (It's hard enough for humans.) It is a fool's errand.

Q: Why is svchost.exe terminating my C# application? A:

The short answer is that svchost.exe did NOT kill your application, or at least it was not the root cause of your app's death. Instead, your app killed itself by crashing or caused its own death by becoming frozen, and in either case the Silent Process Exit Monitor log message is lying to you.

Instead, look in the Application event log for neighboring events from sources "Application Error" or "Application Hang". If those events don't give you enough information, you'll still have to find a way to collect crash dumps from affected users. Sorry about that.

General details

(These details are based on my observation only and Microsoft could change them later.)

When a Windows program crashes, or when the program's windows freeze and the user accepts Windows' offer to forcibly close the program, the Windows Error Reporting (WER) system service intercepts the program exit to collect information about the failing program, including a partial memory dump, so that the failure can be reported to Microsoft's crash telemetry service.

The WER service runs in an svchost.exe process. svchost.exe is a generic program used to run many Windows system services, but if you have Sysinternals Process Monitor/ProcMon running at the time your program crashed, you will know which svchost.exe is WER - it's the one that creates at least one WerFault.exe child process at your program's crash time. The WER svchost.exe's process ID will be the one listed as the killer PID in the Silent Process Exit Monitor log entry in the Application error log, while your own process's decimal PID string will be in the command line of each WerFault.exe helper process.

I'm not sure why Silent Process Exit Monitor blames the WER svchost for killing your process, especially as that log message is itself emitted by WER, which should know better. (The PID of the process that recorded the log message is that of either the WER svchost.exe or one of its WerFault.exe helpers; at least that is the case on my Windows 11 machine.) It's probably just a long-unfixed bug; I would speculate that it is related to WER's usage of the Windows kernel "process snapshotting" feature.

The upshot is that you usually need to ignore Silent Process Exit Monitor log messages that blame svchost.exe for terminating the process. If Silent Process Exit monitoring is turned off for your program, or if the SPE log message blames svchost.exe, look instead for log events from the sources "Application Error" or "Application Hang". If those messages are present and also mention your app's program filename and process ID, then they are the ones to pay attention to, not the messages from "ProcessExitMonitor". (If those messages aren't there, you'll have to check further - it may then be the case that the svchost.exe being blamed is not WER, and that it was genuinely the killer of your process.)

Details specific to the log message you posted

The Silent Process Exit Monitor log message you posted suggests that your program froze and when Windows asked you what to do about it, you chose to forcibly close the program.

You said that the process exit code is 805306369=0x30000001, but that is actually wrong; you missed the - minus sign that negates the value. When you take the signed 32-bit integer -805306369 and treat it as unsigned, you get 0xCFFFFFFF, and that does show up in web searches. (In later versions of Windows, the value gets printed as an unsigned decimal 3489660927, possibly in order to get rid of the sign confusion.)

0xCFFFFFFF is not in the Windows SDK header files, and is not well-documented by Microsoft in general, but it does appear in the Specific Exceptions page within the WinDbg/Debugging Tools for Windows documentation. There it is named STATUS_APPLICATION_HANG and described as "Application hang".

If you write a GUI program that deliberately hangs/freezes, run that program, try to close the frozen app window, and then push "Close the program" in the resulting Windows system dialog, you find that it exits with code 0xCFFFFFFF.

Some additional points

You mentioned that you can't install debugging tools on your customers' PCs, where the crashes happen. Here are some ideas for collecting memory dumps regardless:

  1. If you can, contact affected users to set up dump collection in advance with tools like Sysinternals ProcDump or Windows' built-in WER LocalDumps. If you are already collecting info manually from users, this might be the easiest approach - with WER LocalDumps in particular, the users don't need to download or install anything, which was one of your concerns.
  2. Enroll your company and app in Microsoft's Windows Desktop Application Program and access any minidump CABs for your app that are auto-uploaded to Microsoft.
  3. Add your own dump collection logic and add the result to whatever log or telemetry upload you use.

If you're still uncertain that the svchost.exe really is WER, you can copy C:\Windows\system32\svchost.exe to, say, svchost2.exe, use sc config wersvc to change WER to run under svchost2.exe, and then stop and restart WER. Then you will see svchost2.exe as the process being blamed in the Process Exit Monitor log message. You should then be able to revert the changes.

Thanks to user @Pseudo Random for their answer. I was able to use the additional details to refine my answer, so I disagree with the claim that Pseudo Random's answer was irrelevant and incoherent, even if it is not exactly on point.

Q: How do you solve "Unable to import 'cx_freeze'" - E0401:import-error? A:

I'm returning to this thread to share the solution with those it may help in posterity. The suggestion by @furas was correct. The error was caused by a conflict between two different Python installations on my system. I was able to resolve the error by using a Python Virtual Environment. The virtual environment (venv) installs packages to your project folder thereby keeping the Python installation and its libraries contained from the rest of the system. This is explained in greater detail in this W3Schools article: Due to my relative inexperience with Python, this was my first time learning of venvs.

Q: Access module 'sys' without using import machinery A:

For me, the easiest way to get _import_() is by creating a dummy function.

I don't understand why {}._class_._base_._subclasses_() is needed at all.

This works in both Python 2 and Python 3.

Pyhton 2.7

>>> def f() : pass
... 
>>>f.__globals__['__builtins__'].__import__('sys').version
'2.7.17 (default, Mar  8 2023, 18:40:28) \n[GCC 7.5.0]'
>>>

Python 3 (all versions)

>>> def f() : pass
... 
>>> f.__globals__['__builtins__'].__import__('sys').version
'3.5.2 (default, Nov 12 2018, 13:43:14) \n[GCC 5.4.0 20160609]'
>>>

Python 3.10+

>>> def f() : pass
... 
>>> f.__builtins__['__import__']('sys').version
'3.13.3 (main, Jan 31 2026, 21:48:19) [GCC 7.5.0]'
>>>
